articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

articles.title_orig: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.title_zh: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products.
Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger."
Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider.
Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup.
Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale.
For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago.
"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.
Muse's success was far from inevitable.
Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.
Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.
Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.
That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.
The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.
"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.
Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.
Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."
He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.
When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.
He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.
While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.
Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.
Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.
Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.
The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.
Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.
Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.
"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.
Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.
"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.
At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.
Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.
For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.
"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.

articles.title_orig: The Asian Games should be called the 'China Games' as its domination continues
articles.title_zh: The Asian Games should be called the 'China Games' as its domination continues
articles.content_orig:
NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — They're called the Asian Games . But more aptly, they should be called the “China Games,” another chapter in country’s four-decade domination of the continental, multisports championships.
Midway through the two-week event, China has won 107 gold medals with Japan on 31 in second place. The overall medal total is closer, but China still leads Japan 176 to 129 through Saturday's results.
These Asian Games involve at least 11,000 athletes . That's more than the Summer Olympics two years ago in Paris with about 10,700. And similar to the Olympics, the gap is very wide between the sporting haves, and the have-nots.
At the bottom of the medal table, four countries have only one bronze medal — Bangladesh, Brunei, Mongolia and Syria. And another half dozen countries have yet to win any medals
The six-day swimming competition dominated the first week, and here China piled up 30 golds. Freestyler Zhang Zhanshuo won seven golds and four came in every freestyle distance: the 200-meter, 400, 800 and 1,500. He also added gold in three relays.
Chinese 13-year-old Yu Zidi picked up three golds — 200 butterfly and the 200 and 400 individual medleys. Both swimmers will be forces at the world championships next year in Budapest, Hungary, and the Los Angeles Olympics the year after that.
Despite China's power, the only world record went to Japan's Shin Ohashi , who set the world mark in the 200 breaststroke (2 minutes, 4.83 seconds).
It has been rough sailing for organizers and the Olympic Council of Asia . Organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village, a move to contain spending. Instead, athletes and officials have been lodged on a cruise ship, in hotels, and in temporary wood huts.
Early complaints included beds that are too short, leaky roofs, and mix-ups in room assignment with women booked in with men.
Attendance has also been sparse in some venues, and transportation has been spotty with some venues located far from host city Nagoya.
Organizers have openly apologized.
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport,” Satoshi Murate, organizing committee general secretary, told a Saturday news conference. “I frankly apologize for the mistakes.”
Japan won the bid for these games in 2016. That was before the pandemic, before the Tokyo Olympics were delayed until 2021, and before bid scandals linked to the Tokyo Games were uncovered.
Momentum for big spending was lost.
The final price tag for the Tokyo Olympics was $ 13 billion , though a government audit suggested it was twice that much. In the wake, there was limited interests from sponsors and others to match that spending for the Asian Games.
Organizers were also embarrassed during the first week when the North Korean national anthem was played at a men's field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh.
Chances are you have never seen many of these sports. There's kabaddi, which looks like a physical game of tag, sepaktakraw (foot volleyball), kurash (wrestling with roots in Uzbekistan), jiu jitsu, padel, soft tennis, teqball and wushu.
Of course, there are all the old Olympic standbys such as track and field, tennis, swimming, badminton, gymnastics, soccer, cycling, weightlifting, and so forth.
Esports are also in the Asian Games for the second time following the games in China three years ago. On Saturday 11-year-old Japanese schoolboy Yuki Kurihara won a gold medal.
Mixed martial arts is also being included for the first time with a long-shot eye at landing in the Olympics.
The version in the Asian Games can be described as “MMA Light,” fighting without the cage. Fighters wear gloves and shin pads, elbow blows are banned, and no knees or kicks to the head are allowed when a fighter is on the ground.

articles.title_orig: China’s newest panda diplomats Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are en route to Atlanta
articles.title_zh: China’s newest panda diplomats Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are en route to Atlanta
articles.content_orig:
Two giant pandas have left China on a flight bound for their new home at a zoo in Atlanta, the latest emissaries in Beijing’s long tradition of using “panda diplomacy” to strengthen ties with other countries.
They departed Chengdu, in southwestern China, at 2:55 a.m. Sunday morning local time (2:55 p.m. ET Saturday), China’s state news agency Xinhua said. The flight came just a day after Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington concluded.
During that visit, which was intended to address rising US-China tensions, Xi and US President Donald Trump extended a trade truce and agreed to establish an AI hotline between the two countries.
Video from Xinhua showed fans waving placards as trucks carrying the pandas headed to the airport, from the Giant Panda Breeding Research Base in Sichuan province. Vehicles then towed two crates to the plane before they were lifted into it ahead of their journey, expected to last about 15 hours.
China also arranged for several veterinarians and breeders to remain at the zoo in Atlanta as the pandas enter quarantine upon arrival, the agency added.
The team at Zoo Atlanta and the Chinese team held “many online and offline meetings to carry out in-depth exchanges on the upgrading and transformation plan” for the venue that houses the pandas, which will be on loan from the Chinese government, according to Xinhua.
“What Zoo Atlanta has been working hard for the past year is making improvements to our enclosures, where our enclosures are a lot bigger,” Sam Rivera, the zoo’s vice president of animal health, told Xinhua. “We’re ensuring that we have plenty of bamboo for them to eat. We have experienced keepers that are trained on taking care of giant pandas.”
Rare, fluffy and irresistibly cute, pandas are adored across the globe. The animals once roamed a vast swath of China, along with parts of northern Myanmar and Vietnam, but human encroachment and climate change shrank the habitat of the bamboo-munching bears to just six mountain ranges above the Sichuan basin, deep in China’s hinterland.
Hailed in imperial times as the “land of heavenly abundance,” Sichuan is now better known as the “hometown of pandas.” The mountainous province boasts a latticework of panda nature reserves and breeding centers, all built in recent decades as China – and the world – raced to save the multimillion-years-old “living fossil” from extinction.
Provincial capital Chengdu – a sprawling metropolis known for its spicy hotpot and old tea houses – sits at the foot of snow-capped mountains with misty old-growth forests where wild pandas still roam.
The city’s panda breeding base is the largest in the country, housing more than 240 bears – or a third of the world’s captive panda population. The sprawling facility draws up to 11 million visitors a year, on par with Shanghai Disneyland.
Loaning pandas has long been a tool of Chinese diplomacy, following a decades-long government effort to transform them from a little-known animal into a cultural icon and national symbol. For more than half a century, Beijing has dispatched these charismatic animals overseas to shore up alliances, mend estranged ties and court new partners.
“The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans,” Xi said on Thursday , referencing the half-century in which pandas lived in US zoos on loan from the Chinese government. That tradition was started by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1972, shortly after Richard Nixon became the first US president to visit China following the Communist Party’s rise to power in 1949.
One of the pandas bound for Atlanta even has the same name – Ping Ping, meaning “peace” – as the first ever panda Mao gifted to the Soviet Union in 1957. He was born on March 17, 2020, has large black patches around his eyes and is especially good at climbing trees, according to China’s National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
China is more in love with its pandas than ever. That’s complicated matters for Beijing
The other panda, Fu Shuang, meaning “double blessings,” was born seven months later on October 18. She has a small tuft of fur on the top of her head, a slightly protruding forehead and finds food very easily, the administration said.
In a report ahead of their upcoming journey, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV asked their keeper to describe the pair.
Ping Ping “is brave and gentle,” Fu Jia said. “During training sessions, when he spots me holding an apple, he will make soft whimpering sounds, eager for the treat.”
Fu Shuang, on the other hand, “is crazy about honey,” she said.
Zookeepers at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding selected the pair after considering their age, health, genetics and personality.
“They should be docile and like each other, and hopefully be able to mate naturally,” the park’s deputy director Li Mingxi told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
They are scheduled to arrive in Atlanta early on Sunday morning local time. The zoo has hosted several pandas before. Another pair, Lun Lun and Yang Yang, had seven offspring there between 2006 and 2016 before returning to Chengdu.
Zoo Atlanta earlier in the year said it would be “delighted and honored” to welcome the two pandas.
A banner displayed at the zoo on Saturday read “The future home of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang.”
A Zoo Atlanta representative said the facility would not share information about Ping Ping and Fu Shuang’s planned arrival date, and declined to comment further.
Chinese officials and the Atlanta zoo “will carry out in-depth academic and cultural exchanges to continuously enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the people of China and the United States,” Xinhua said.
Panda diplomacy has offered some relief from the tensions increasingly shaping the US-China relationship in recent years, as the two countries compete in an AI arms race and engage in a spiraling trade war.
Two giant pandas arrived in San Diego in June 2024, the first time China allowed new pandas to travel to the US in more than two decades. A second pair traveled to Washington’s National Zoo later that year.
In preparation for the move, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang have been quarantined for a month with a roster of live-in carers, Li said. The pandas have been trained for their long flight too, becoming used to their crate and loud noises.
Late Saturday night, China’s ambassador to the US Xie Feng shared photos of the two pandas on his X account and said they were on their way.
“Get ready to greet our two fluffy stars!” he wrote.
Their departure would be a sad one for, Fu, their keeper.
“After caring for them for so long… It’s like raising your own children,” she told CCTV.
“They weighed barely over 100 grams at birth, and we nurtured them until they grew big and heavy. I won’t get to see them for quite a long time, so it’s hard to say goodbye.”
CNN’s Xiaoqian Lin, Farida Elsebai, Rebekah Riess, Eduardo Cuevas and Mitchell McCluskey contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: USC loses to Oregon in yet another broken promise of the Lincoln Riley era
articles.title_zh: USC loses to Oregon in yet another broken promise of the Lincoln Riley era
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
It was nearly a half decade ago  that Lincoln Riley , dressed in a slick blue suit and glossy cardinal tie, stood atop the Coliseum’s rooftop deck, grinning as he gazed out across the field below. He’d just been introduced as USC’s new head coach, and in that moment, anything felt possible for the future of Trojan football. Riley, at the time, was one of the most renowned young coaches in college football. And as he surveyed the scene, he painted the picture of a day when the Trojans were back on top and the Coliseum was hallowed ground once again.
“This place,” Riley said that day, “is going to be the mecca of college football .”
But less than five years later, as final seconds ticked away on a 41-27 loss to Oregon on Saturday, fans trudged toward the exits, many of them surely wondering how much longer they’d accept the current state of USC football.
That moment of truth wouldn’t come Saturday. The first loss for the Trojans at the Coliseum since 2024 wouldn’t spell the end of their season by any means — not after a single defeat to No. 20 Oregon — but in that moment, the future that Riley had envisioned felt as far away as ever.
USC delivered a late hit that knocked Oregon quarterback Dante Moore out of the game early, but the Ducks rallied for a 41-27 road win Saturday.
Riley tried afterwards to plead otherwise: “We have a damn good football team,” he said. “I know we do.”
There will still be chances for the Trojans to prove their coach right. But the stakes on Saturday had arguably never been higher for USC’s coach, who spent all offseason explaining how this season would be different. There were no more excuses, no more explanations for why USC was still falling short — even he seemed to agree to that. Everything he’d been pointing towards in the distance was now here, culminating all at once.
With a gauntlet of a Big Ten schedule ahead, there was no better time for Riley to prove he had USC moving in the right direction and no better matchup to help catapult the Trojans into the College Football Playoff conversation than Oregon, its newest — and still maybe most bitter — rival. The whole college football world was watching, waiting to see if USC’s coach could deliver in the most critical of moments.
Instead, Riley and his Trojans ended up as the punchline in Oregon coach Dan Lanning’s postgame news conference.
“Three wins against these guys,” Lanning said. “I guess if you’re from this area and you’re interested in winning football games, you should go to Oregon. If you’re interested in going to a Chris Brown concert, you should go here.”
The Trojans once again were in an all-too-familiar, all-too-painful position, one they’d experienced many times before during Riley’s tenure. Mistakes piled up. Ill-timed penalties too. And worst of all, USC’s defense still couldn’t get a stop. It gave up 504 yards to Oregon, the third-most it had allowed over the past three seasons.
The Ducks would score on six of their last seven drives, almost all of which featured their backup quarterback at the helm. That was after Oregon star quarterback Dante Moore was knocked out of the game early in the second quarter following a brutal hit by USC linebacker Desman Stephens II . The hit, which Lanning called “disgusting” after the game, started a shoving match between players from both teams.
Stephens, who was seen celebrating after the play, was kicked out of the game, but he remained on the sideline in the second half.
Riley said after the game that he didn’t see Stephens celebrating. And when asked why he stayed on the sideline, Riley responded, “Why? Because he’s on our football team.”
The play cast a pall over the rest of the game, but Oregon backup quarterback Dylan Raiola managed to throw for 289 yards and two touchdowns against USC’s defense. Jayden Maiava, meanwhile, had 326 yards and two touchdowns, but completed just 23 of 42 passes.
The rushing attack wasn’t much better, as the Trojans averaged a mere 3.6 yards per carry.
The game began on a bitter note for USC. After marching on a 13-play opening drive, a third-down sack forced the Trojans to settle for a field-goal attempt. But Caden Chittenden missed an easy kick wide right. It was just the latest in a string of recent special teams slip-ups for the Trojans.
Why has it been so hard for USC football to compete for a national title after setting the standard in college football during Pete Carroll’s tenure?
The defense, however, held early, even after Oregon running back Jordon Davison burst out of the backfield for a 45-yard run on the Ducks’ first play. Oregon finished that drive with a field goal, the only points either high-scoring offense managed in the first quarter.
Unable to get anything going on the ground, the Trojans turned to their stud freshman receiver to pace the offense. Five of Maiava’s first seven completions went to Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, one of which came on a 31-yard strike down the seam for a touchdown despite tight coverage.
Oregon was mounting a response when Moore took off on a quarterback scramble. But as he slid, Stephens decked Moore with a direct hit to his helmet, even after he had already given himself up. Moore spent several minutes on the field before being loaded onto a cart and taken to Los Angeles General Medical Center by ambulance.
Lanning said after the game that Moore had movement in all of his extremities while at the hospital. His absence left Raiola, the backup, to take the reins of Oregon’s offense, and he led the Ducks to the doorstep of the goal line.
USC’s defense stood tall in the red zone that time, holding Oregon to a field goal. But it wouldn’t last.
Raiola proceeded to find his rhythm in the second half. He led the Ducks on consecutive touchdown drives in just 11 plays.
USC responded with three straight scoring drives, and even added a stop from its defense in between. The third — an 11-yard strike to Tanook Hines — tied the score 27-27 with less than 13 minutes remaining.
USC looked to have Oregon stopped in its tracks on the ensuing possession. Then, on a third-and-long incompletion, defensive tackle Jide Abasiri was flagged for roughing the passer. The penalty gave Oregon just the opening it needed.
“We had all the momentum in the world,” Riley said. “But you can’t do that against good teams and good offenses.”
The Ducks scored five plays later, as Raiola lofted a prayer to the corner of the end zone that was answered by one of his wideouts, Dakorien Moore.
A failed fourth-down attempt for the Trojans, with the Ducks leading 34-27, would all but end it.
Maiava’s desperation pass was swatted away. And with it, so too were any assumptions that this season at USC would be much different than the four that came before it.

articles.title_zh: The Asian Games should be called the 'China Games' as its domination continues
articles.content_orig:
China's Song Jiayuan, right, and Zhang Linru hold their flags after competing in the women's shot put final at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Credit: AP/Lee Jin-man
NAGOYA, Japan — They're called the Asian Games. But more aptly, they should be called the “China Games,” another chapter in country’s four-decade domination of the continental, multisports championships.
Midway through the two-week event, China has won 107 gold medals with Japan on 31 in second place. The overall medal total is closer, but China still leads Japan 176 to 129 through Saturday's results.
These Asian Games involve at least 11,000 athletes. That's more than the Summer Olympics two years ago in Paris with about 10,700. And similar to the Olympics, the gap is very wide between the sporting haves, and the have-nots.
At the bottom of the medal table, four countries have only one bronze medal — Bangladesh, Brunei, Mongolia and Syria. And another half dozen countries have yet to win any medals
The six-day swimming competition dominated the first week, and here China piled up 30 golds. Freestyler Zhang Zhanshuo won seven golds and four came in every freestyle distance: the 200-meter, 400, 800 and 1,500. He also added gold in three relays.

Chinese 13-year-old Yu Zidi picked up three golds — 200 butterfly and the 200 and 400 individual medleys. Both swimmers will be forces at the world championships next year in Budapest, Hungary, and the Los Angeles Olympics the year after that.
Despite China's power, the only world record went to Japan's Shin Ohashi, who set the world mark in the 200 breaststroke (2 minutes, 4.83 seconds).
The flags of China and Japan are raised during the medal ceremony for the men's rings final in artistic gymnastics at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Eugene Hoshiko
It has been rough sailing for organizers and the Olympic Council of Asia. Organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village, a move to contain spending. Instead, athletes and officials have been lodged on a cruise ship, in hotels, and in temporary wood huts.
Early complaints included beds that are too short, leaky roofs, and mix-ups in room assignment with women booked in with men.
Attendance has also been sparse in some venues, and transportation has been spotty with some venues located far from host city Nagoya.
Organizers have openly apologized.
Gold medalist, China team, pose with their national flag, after the women's 4 x 200-meter freestyle relay final in swimming at the Asian Games in Tokyo, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Hiro Komae
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport,” Satoshi Murate, organizing committee general secretary, told a Saturday news conference. “I frankly apologize for the mistakes.”
Japan won the bid for these games in 2016. That was before the pandemic, before the Tokyo Olympics were delayed until 2021, and before bid scandals linked to the Tokyo Games were uncovered.
Momentum for big spending was lost.
The final price tag for the Tokyo Olympics was $ 13 billion, though a government audit suggested it was twice that much. In the wake, there was limited interests from sponsors and others to match that spending for the Asian Games.
Organizers were also embarrassed during the first week when the North Korean national anthem was played at a men's field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh.
Chances are you have never seen many of these sports. There's kabaddi, which looks like a physical game of tag, sepaktakraw (foot volleyball), kurash (wrestling with roots in Uzbekistan), jiu jitsu, padel, soft tennis, teqball and wushu.
Of course, there are all the old Olympic standbys such as track and field, tennis, swimming, badminton, gymnastics, soccer, cycling, weightlifting, and so forth.
Esports are also in the Asian Games for the second time following the games in China three years ago. On Saturday 11-year-old Japanese schoolboy Yuki Kurihara won a gold medal.
Mixed martial arts is also being included for the first time with a long-shot eye at landing in the Olympics.
The version in the Asian Games can be described as “MMA Light,” fighting without the cage. Fighters wear gloves and shin pads, elbow blows are banned, and no knees or kicks to the head are allowed when a fighter is on the ground.

Week 4 boasted the best slate of games on paper of the 2026 season to date, and the action on the field lived up to the hype with the cream rising to the top in ranked showdowns across the country.
The story of the day was No. 20 Oregon going on the road and taking down No. 12 USC, 41-27. The Ducks were road favorites against their long-time rivals, but after star quarterback Dante Moore left the game on a stretcher after a violent late hit on a slide, no one was quite sure what Oregon would look like with backup Dylan Raiola.
The answer was "incredible," as Raiola threw for 289 yards and two touchdowns in a phenomenal performance stepping in suddenly for the injured Moore to lead the Ducks to a much-needed victory. Moore was taken to a local hospital and had feeling in his extremities after the scary hit to his head, but his status going forward remains in question as he undergoes further testing and evaluation.
The Big Ten had a pair of surprising upsets earlier in the day, with No. 17 Iowa taking down No. 18 Michigan 20-19 in The Big House on a last-second touchdown pass. Then No. 13 Penn State got stunned at home by Wisconsin in a 24-20 loss after the Badgers hit a 70-yard touchdown in the closing minutes to pull off a massive upset.
In the SEC, No. 1 Texas survived a road test agaainst No. 14 Tennessee in a 20-17 win that included a wild finish where the Volunteers had a chance to tie or win after getting an onside kick but could not get into range. No. 21 Florida then blew out No. 4 Ole Miss, 52-28, running all over the Rebels in another dominant offensive performance to remain undefeated and hand Ole Miss its first loss.
In the evening, No. 10 LSU dominated No. 23 Texas A&M in a 35-6 rout, setting off alarm bells in College Station after a second straight lopsided loss. The other ranked battle in the SEC featured two surprise teams, as No. 24 Mississippi State outlasted No. 19 Missouri, 31-24, behind another phenomenal performance from this year's breakout star at quarterback, Kamario Taylor.

Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor capped a five-play, 85-yard drive with a 24-yard touchdown pass with 3:57 to play to give the Bulldogs their first top-25 win for his program since 2014. Taylor finished with 360 yards passing and three touchdowns, his fourth straight start with three or more touchdown passes — a first in program history.
Taylor led consecutive touchdown drives in the fourth quarter after his team had fallen behind 24-17 in the second half. Mississippi State is 4-0 in consecutive seasons for the first time since 1944-45.
The Bulldogs had just one SEC win over Jeff Lebby's first two seasons as coach and are now 2-0 in the conference this season.
"We're trying to take the next step and we've got so much out in front of us," Lebby said.
When Oregon saw star quarterback Dante Moore leave the game on a stretcher in the second quarter trailing 10-7, there were serious concerns for the Ducks in both the short- and long-term. Then backup Dylan Raiola stepped in and kept the Ducks' offense rolling, leading five touchdown drives for the Ducks in a dominant performance in the Coliseum, as they eventually pulled away from the Trojans for a 14-point win.
Raiola finished the game 19-of-25 for 289 yards and two touchdowns in a wildly impressive showing after being thrust into action suddenly. The win keeps Oregon's hopes of competing for a Big Ten title and a College Football Playoff berth alive, and Raiola's individual performance provides optimism that he can keep the Ducks at that elite level for however long Moore's absence lasts. Moore had feeling in his extremities after taking a vicious late hit on a slide, but was taken to a hospital for evaluations and we won't know more on his condition until they're don with testing and examinations.
On the other side, it's the continuation of a frustrating trend at USC, where they've been outclassed by top competition in the Lincoln Riley era. The defense had no answers for the Ducks and while Jayden Maiava kept the Trojans in it as long as he could, the offense wasn't quite sharp enough to keep pace in a shootout. Now Riley will face tough questions in what felt like a make or break year as the Trojans get set to hit the meat of their Big Ten schedule with some tough opponents on the horizon including Ohio State and Indiana.
It's been a back-and-forth affair all night in Starkville, but Kamario Taylor has put the home team on top with an incredible sequence of throws in the first quarter. After a deep ball down the left sideline to a fully laid out Anthony Evans III, Taylor threw a dart over the middle to Sanfrisco Magee to put the Bulldogs on top with under four to play.
Now it's on Austin Simmons to find the answer for Mizzou in what's been one of the most entertaining games of the night.
The shootout in the Coliseum continues with another touchdown pass from Dylan Raiola. The Oregon backup has come in and stepped up in a big way, with his latest touchdown on a moon ball to Dakorien Moore, who shook free of the corner and then was able to rise up for a contested catch as the ball hung in the air for seemingly forever before getting to him.
Perhaps more impressive than the Ducks scoring again on USC's porous defense is that they were able to get a stop on the ensuing USC drive, stopping a 4th and 7 attempt by USC at midfield to take over with a chance to go up two scores.
The last time Oklahoma State won a Big 12 conference game was Nov. 25, 2023, when Alan Bowman was quarterback and Ollie Gordon was a first-year starter. Nearly three years later, the 18-game conference losing streak is over after the Cowboys overcame an early deficit to beat West Virginia 41-24.
Cowboys wide receiver Wyatt Young took over the game in the second half, finishing with eight catches for 192 yards and a touchdown out of the slot. Quarterback Drew Mestemaker had 274 passing yards in the second half alone. West Virginia rushed for an absurd 334 yards, but the Cowboys locked down in the fourth quarter to pull away.
After shaking off a slow start, Austin Simmons has asserted himself in Starkville.

Lee has been rolling as well. He's up to seven catches for 93 yards and two touchdowns.

articles.title_zh: ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts
articles.content_orig:
After eight years and countless entries in the expanding onscreen universe, Star Wars is revisiting the Skywalker family with its next project.
Deadline can confirm that Lucasfilm has tapped Skeleton Crew co-creator Jon Watts (director of Spider-Man: Homecoming , Spider-Man: Far From Home and Spider-Man: No Way Home ) to helm the first installment in a new trilogy of the Skywalker Saga, which is being penned by Simon Kinberg ( X-Men: Dark Phoenix , Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith ).
Kinberg, who previously co-created the DisneyXD animated series Star Wars Rebels (2014-’18), has been working on the new trilogy since 2018, with Daisy Ridley reportedly eyed to reprise her role as Rey, as it will serve in the next chapter of the Skywalker Saga.
The project reportedly has not yet received a greenlight from parent company Disney.
Beginning with Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope in 1977 and the sequels Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Episode VI — Return of the Jedi (1983), the Skywalker Saga continued with the prequel trilogy Episode I — The Phantom Menace (1999), Episode II: Attack of the Clones (2002) and Episode III — Revenge of the Sith (2005).
Most recently, the franchise left off the Skywalker Saga with the latest trilogy, Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens (2015), Episode VIII — The Last Jedi (2017) and Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker (2019), which was led by Ridley’s Rey.
Since the last chapter in the Skywalker Saga, the Star Wars franchise has expanded with films and streaming series set throughout the onscreen universe, with the next installment Star Wars: Starfighter set for a May 28, 2027 premiere.
Lucasfilm had no comment. Knight Edge Media was first to report the news.
Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy.
Star Wars was never a franchise. It was a serialized story told over six films, based on the interests and inspirations of one very peculiar individual. Whatever you think of his craft, Lucas was focused on delivering a grand mythology, which foregrounded a family tragedy against an epic background of fantasy, adventure and political allegory. No one other than him has delivered anything remotely like it in the history of the medium.
Expecting that anyone else could do the same was Disney’s big mistake. In fact, like many observers and even some fans, they fundamentally misunderstood what made the saga so successful. Handing it over to people who also didn’t get it like Abrams – who basically approached the job as a fanboy – ended in retread, deconstruction and chaos.
You can expand on ideas in the story, like Gilroy did to great effect, or you can tell adventure stories backward or forward in time, but none of it is going to get you the same unexpected epic that only Lucas was uniquely placed to tell. So, yeah, I expect it’s going to be a slow death for the property, as no new story / idea emerges to inspire people all over again.
Wow that sounds bad. Like every part of it
Rey is a Palpatine. Disney offed all the Skywalkers in their terrible fanfic and named SW after the now gone Skywalkers like a developer naming a street Oak Street after getting rid of all the oaks. Hopefully Star Wars’ good name can be free some day.
“Star Wars Continuing the Skywalker Saga with Spider-Man” would generate a lot more interest.
Dropping all their plans and going after a top tier filmmaker in Christopher Nolan should have been the play. Giving him total creative freedom. But they’re unwilling to learn. Maybe they need another decade of failure to get it.
I remember seeing a video of Nolan during the Oppenheimer press tour, where he had to give yes or no answers. When he got the obligatory “Would you do a Star Wars film?”, he just said “Pass.”
Given he’s not made a franchise film since he parted ways with Batman, I can’t ever see Nolan going back to franchise work. He has all the power any director would want. He’s not going to give that away to play in someone else’s sandbox.

articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.content_orig:
US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.
The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.
Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.
Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.
During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.
In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.
That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.
Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.
After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.
Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.
He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.
This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.
Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.
The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.
Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.
Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.
Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

articles.title_zh: Iran says it will wait for official US response after Trump rejects Strait of Hormuz proposal
articles.content_orig:
Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days.
In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements.
Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly".
On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries.
Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June.
Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.
The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it.
Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said.
Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.
Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.
Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker.
Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".
"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran.
Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.
The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.
These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Powerful Nor’easter digs in on the East Coast
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Powerful Nor’easter digs in on the East Coast
articles.content_orig:
A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.
Tens of millions of people were in the path of the nor'easter, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. Around 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.
In Brooklyn, New York, a 56-year-old man was struck and killed by a falling tree, according to the New York City Police Department, the first confirmed fatality from the storm. The New York City Housing Authority later confirmed he was an employee of the agency. He was identified by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a social media post as Leighton Brown.
And in Egg Harbor Township in eastern New Jersey, nine adults and a dog were rescued from flooded motel rooms.
The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There will be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
Rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches are expected from the Philadelphia region into eastern New Jersey, and portions of Long Island and southern New England could see 3 to 5 inches of rain.
The nor'easter is rapidly intensifying and is expected to make a sharp turn back toward the New Jersey coast Saturday night into Sunday. It may stall or meander nearby through Monday, prolonging the rain, wind and coastal impacts before finally departing on Tuesday.
In Long Island, New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, Kenny Formica sat at his home watching surveillance cameras showing water rising inside the marina he owns. Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.
Ahead of the storm, Formica said workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm's way and parked the marina's trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.
Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. One customer sent him a video around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot boat after it had blown off its lift.
"This is like an 8,000-pound boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.
In Ocean City, Maryland, heavy surf caused beach erosion, washed out fencing by the dunes and was leading to flooding.
"In all the canals, the water is up really high and coming into people's backyards," Jay Boyd said by telephone.
Further south, Ellie Hodge stood on her front stoop in Norfolk, Virginia, on Saturday and watched as passing vehicles left wakes. The coastal city has seen isolated flooding all week because of the nor'easter.
"We've seen cars get stuck on the road, going up the sidewalks," Hodge said. "It's been pretty bad this time around."
The storm forced a change of plans for many people. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
The New Jersey and Delaware coasts could see wind gusts of about 60 miles per hour, though meteorologists have already seen reports of winds over 70 miles per hour. Inland, residents could see wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph.
Eastern Long Island and southeastern New England could see gusts of 45 to 65 mph.
Peak wind gusts for Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket could approach 60 to 65 miph on Friday night and Saturday, NWS meteorologist Matthew Belk said.
Inland residents will see wind gusts of about 50 to 55 mph, Belk said.
"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.
The early timing of the nor'easter in the season could lead to even more damaging effects. Because trees are still fully leafed, they will have more wind resistance, Belk said. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which, combined with the saturated ground caused by heavy rain, could cause power outages, leave debris on roads and lead to other property damage.
Strong winds could also push ocean waves over seawalls, creating flooding. Large waves and elevated water levels could also lead to beach erosion and sand dune breaches.
On Massachusetts' South Shore, the towns of Cohasset and Scituate were sitting right in the bullseye of the storm. While parts of the coastline are protected by seawalls, some of those seawalls are in the middle of repair projects or have seen those projects stall due to federal funding cuts .
"So the waves hit the seawall and they go straight up about 60, 70, 80 feet, and the wind hits it from the northeast and every wave ends up hitting the house," Kevin Gill, owner of an oceanfront Scituate home, told CBS News Boston on Thursday.
The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — both gearing up for the playoffs during the final weekend of the regular Major League Baseball season — had to shuffle the schedule for their three-game series. They played a double-header Friday in Boston to try to avoid the storm. Then MLB rescheduled their finale on Sunday to occur in Florida, at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays.
Ed Sheeran canceled his high-profile concerts Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Also canceled: an Ironman triathlon in New York and the three-day Oceans Calling Festival in Ocean City, Maryland, which had been promoted online as "a wave of music."
Farther south, a highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's Saturday wedding plans. The Virginia couple had made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported. A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music. Organizers invited anyone on the island to come celebrate with the couple Saturday afternoon.
In New York City, the Global Citizens Festival and All Things Go NYC were canceled ahead of the storm.
The nor'easter also caused hundreds of flight cancellations and delays. The flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 260 flight cancellations for Boston Logan International Airport as of early Saturday evening.
State officials along the East Coast urged people to use caution. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but the storm will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet.
"The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said early Saturday.
In Long Island, ferry owner Stephanie Sherman said she had paused operations between Patchogue and the barrier island of Fire Island.
"It's been a pretty wild storm," Sherman said. "But nothing that we haven't experienced in the past. These happen every so often."
Nikki  Nolan and Andrew  Kozak contributed to this report.

Indonesia is considering Chinese investment to help build a massive 2,772km (1,722 mile) railway network through the vast, resource-rich region of Kalimantan, following the completion of Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung, state media and analysts said.
However, analysts noted that any future commercial agreements were likely to be negotiated cautiously, given the financial strains that dogged the high-speed line and the challenges that stalled a proposed underground metro project in the congested tourist province of Bali.
The Indonesian government was “exploring” potential foreign investment to build the Trans-Kalimantan railway network, according to statements from Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi quoted by Indonesia’s official Antara news agency. The minister said China and Russia had expressed interest in the project.

Niger Stress Its Sovereignty and Thanks Algeria
Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine portrayed his West African nation and neighboring military-run Sahel states as a last rampart of African independence against European neocolonialism in his speech on Friday, Sept. 25, at the General Assembly.
His remarks echoed his address at the high-level week last year, blaming most of his country’s problems on France, except that this year’s address singled out its northern neighbor, Algeria, for praise.
“The AES is to Africa, its historical and contemporary diasporas, what light is to darkness. It is a beacon of hope and dignity for this human community present in all four corners of the world,” he said, referring to the Alliance of Sahel States : Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.
On Aug. 29-30, 2026, Nigerien soldiers mutinied and attacked the main airport military base in the capital, Niamey, and the national TV station. Fighting broke out in the streets near the presidential palace between soldiers loyal to the current military government and soldiers criticizing the current government for poor governance and growing insecurity.
The government, led by a former head of the presidential guard, Gen. Abourahamane Tiani, defeated the mutinous soldiers with the help of Russian soldiers based in Niger. Zeine referenced the attack in his General Assembly speech, saying that “a third attempt at destabilization, led by obscurantist and colonialist forces, targeted our institutions. Like the previous ones, it failed, thanks to the loyalty of our Armed Forces.”
Niger has since reorganized its military hierarchy, including changing the chief of staff of the armed forces from a brigade general who was trained by the American military to someone closer to General Tiani.
General Tiani took power in a coup against the elected President Mohamed Bazoum in 2023 and has kept him in house arrest in Niamey since then, proclaiming himself as head of the “transitional government.” With no timeline on the length of the transition, critics have argued that he is aiming to remain head of state for the foreseeable future.
Although Algeria had condemned Tiani’s 2023 coup, it has increased ties with Niger in the last year. After the attempted August mutiny, Algeria sent four Sukhoi Su-30MKA fighter jets, a refueling tanker and a transport plane to Niamey in an unprecedented show of force and support for the Nigerien government.
Algeria reportedly intervened partly out of concern for the United Arab Emirates’ enhanced engagement in the Sahel region and support for the military leader Khalifa Haftar in eastern Libya. He is accused of supporting rebel groups in northern Niger. Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the UAE on Sept. 10, 2026.
Indeed, toward the end of his speech, Zeine heaped praise on Algeria, saying that Niger “is standing on its own feet today because the People’s Democratic Republic of Algeria, a brotherly and neighboring country, has chosen to support it through substantial investment in the exploitation of its natural resources and through constant support for its defense system.
With Algeria, we also maintain dynamic cooperation in the fields of health, education, energy, water resources, and agriculture.” — Dulcie Leimbach
Sweden’s Minister for Foreign Affairs Maria Malmer Stenergard began her remarks to the 81st General Assembly, on Sept. 25, with a story about her grandmother, Alice, who grew up in rural Sweden and became an exemplar of women’s independence and financial literacy through her work at a local bank.
Through this anecdote, Stenergard emphasized that many women remain economically dependent on men, arguing that “women’s economic empowerment is a matter of freedom.” Referencing her grandmother, she noted that both Sweden and Afghanistan granted women the right to vote in 1919, yet the contrast in women’s freedoms between the two countries is now stark.
“Freedoms do not defend themselves. It is up to us to protect them, for women and girls everywhere,” she said.
Stenegard connected those rights to growing global challenges to sovereignty and territorial integrity, pointing to the rising number of armed conflicts and civilian suffering in a range of places, including Ukraine, Palestine, Lebanon, Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
She focused most sharply on Russia’s four-year-old war in Ukraine, calling the invasion “a blatant violation of international law” and accusing Russia of violating the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and human rights law. She cited attacks on civilians, the forcible deportation of children, torture and conflict-related sexual violence.
“Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial,” she said, arguing that “there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability.”
Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov directly, Stenergard said: “The path to peace is clear, the choice should be easy. Withdraw your troops. End this war.”
Stenergard also sought to reinforce Sweden’s longstanding relationship with the UN, pointing to the role of Swedish peacekeepers, mediators and development assistance in the organization. Sweden, she said, would remain “a staunch partner” while pushing for a UN that is “more effective, more transparent and better equipped to uphold the principles of its Charter.”
She ended with a quote by the late Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold, another Swede, she said, “The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one — not the military strength, but the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of people — is indirectly the strength of all.” — Miriam Alrahil
China Stands Up for Gaza and Cuba
Chinese Vice President Han Zheng addressed the 81st session of the General Assembly on Saturday, soon after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit with President Trump at the White House this week.
During the Washington summit, Xi emphasized the need for China and the US to “co-exist in peace,” saying that both countries can gain from cooperation but lose from confrontation. Against this backdrop, Han’s 12-minute speech on Sept. 26 echoed Xi’s message, with peace at its center.
Han called for greater international cooperation and the preservation of peace amid growing geopolitical tensions and global challenges. He emphasized the importance of the UN-centered international system and international law, calling on countries to resolve disputes through dialogue and consultation rather than military action.
Regarding the Mideast, Han advocated for respecting the sovereignty and security of countries in the region. He called for Gaza’s postwar reconstruction to follow the principle of “Palestinians governing Palestine” and urged a return to the path of a two-state solution. A year ago, 142 countries in the General Assembly endorsed a declaration to reinforce the longstanding but unacted approach to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Han also addressed Cuba, which has endured a decades-old US embargo as well as new punishing economic measures by the US. He called for the US to end threats of force against Cuba and urged the immediate, complete lifting of the blockade and sanctions imposed by the US on the Caribbean country. His remarks reflected Beijing’s broader emphasis on avoiding confrontation and promoting stability in its relations with Washington.
On global development, an overriding focus of China at the UN, Han highlighted the matters of poverty reduction, food security, energy transition and climate finance across the world. In China’s role as a major voice of the global South, Han called for more financial and other support for developing countries and emphasized maintaining global trade and stable supply chains.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square
articles.content_orig:
LOURDES, France (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is taking his opposition to euthanasia and medically assisted dying to Lourdes , the French Catholic shrine associated with miraculous cures and now also a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse.
Leo was to meet with French bishops on Sunday and then celebrate Mass on the prairie in front of Lourdes' main basilica before an estimated 150,000 people. Later in the day, Leo was to meet with a group of survivors in what has become a regular appointment in papal trips.
Lourdes became a major pilgrimage destination after the Catholic Church officially recognized visions of the Virgin Mary reported here by a young girl in 1858.
The site near the Spanish border draws millions of pilgrims each year, especially sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from the famed spring water in the Lourdes grotto where the visions purportedly occurred.
Leo arrived in Lourdes on Saturday night from Paris and immediately prayed inside the Grotto of Apparitions and drank from the spring.
During his four-day visit to France, Leo has repeatedly called for a renewed respect for life in keeping with Catholic teaching that all human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death. The teaching translates into firm opposition to abortion and medically assisted dying.
France's National Assembly in 2024 enshrined abortion as a constitutional right and recently gave final approval to a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
In Lourdes, where the church has recognized as authentic 72 "miraculous" cures, the question of respecting even the most frail, sick and vulnerable is particularly acute.
More recently, Lourdes has also become a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse. Leo was to meet with seven victims on Sunday, including one who was abused as an adult, in recognition of the new frontier of the abuse crisis that the church faces.
The French church has endured a brutal reckoning with its legacy of abuse. An independent report in 2021 estimated 330,000 children had been abused over 70 years by some 3,000 priests and church workers.
Despite criticism of the report's methodology and conclusions, French bishops put in place an independent system of compensation for victims that to date has recommended the church pay out more than 20 million euros ($22.7 million).
On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of victims wrote an open letter asking him to acknowledge the church's responsibility and criticizing that the seven survivors were chosen by the church, not victims' groups. "The Church must relinquish its position as both judge and party to the proceedings," they wrote in the letter published by French newspaper Liberation.
In Lourdes, Leo will also be reminded of a prickly abuse case inherited from Pope Francis.
The façade of one of the Lourdes basilicas was designed by the Rev. Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic Church's most famous mosaic artists.
Rupnik is currently on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them starting in the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks.
His case was covered up for three decades by his Jesuit superiors , and even Francis was suspected of having protected his fellow Jesuit. In response to a media outcry, Francis in 2024 ordered a canonical trial, which is ongoing .
The Rupnik case posed the question of what to do with his mosaics, which adorn basilicas around the world.
In 2024, Lourdes Bishop Jean-Marc Micas decided to no longer illuminate the façade of the Notre Dame du Rosaire Basilica at night. He subsequently ordered the decorated doors covered, and more recently decided to cover the façade's mosaics entirely. He reasoned that abuse victims who come to Lourdes for healing shouldn't be forced to see them.
As Leo approached the grotto on Saturday night, his popemobile drove by the basilica and its boarded up mosaics.

articles.title_orig: Iowa beats the clock, flips Michigan’s Big House magic on its head with late touchdown pass
articles.title_zh: Iowa beats the clock, flips Michigan’s Big House magic on its head with late touchdown pass
articles.content_orig:
Hank Brown and Iowa found a way to leave thousands of Michigan fans shocked with thrilling victory.
Somehow, Iowa football pulled it off inside the Big House in Ann Arbor against Michigan .
Hank Brown led a game-winning drive, finding Reece Vander Zee on a touchdown strike as time expired. The Hawkeyes secured a 20-19 victory over the Wolverines in the Big Ten Conference opener.
If anyone doubted Brown and his abilities, those doubts were put to rest. In one drive, the Auburn transfer made believers out of all Iowa fans watching.
Related: 3 Takeaways From Iowa 55-0 Dismantling Of Northern Iowa
Here are three takeaways from Iowa's stunning win over Michigan in Big Ten Conference play.
No matter what Hank Brown does from here on out, Hawkeye fans will never forget him. Brown finished 21 of 35 for 227 yards, throwing two touchdowns vs. Michigan. That included an 11-play, 91-yard drive for the game-winning score.
Brown quickly led Iowa down the field against the Wolverine defense. They covered those 91 yards in 106 seconds, leaving no time on the clock.
He had six completions on the drive to win it. That included a 29-yard pass with two seconds left to position the game-winning throw ot Vander Zee.
Much like his quarterback, Reece Vander Zee will be remembered for this. Vander Zee, a former Iowa high school standout, made a highlight-reel catch for the winning score.
Vander Zee dragged both feet and hauled in the pass from Brown from 16 yards out. He also had a key 12-yard catch for a first down earlier in the drive to end the game.
He led the Hawkeyes with five receptions for 66 yards. Vander Zee also caught a 16-yard pass for a score from Brown in the fourth quarter to put Iowa ahead, 14-13.
Remember when opponents were scared of Cooper DeJean in the return game? Another former Iowa high school football standout just might have caused flashbacks of the current Philadelphia Eagles star.
Braeden Jackson, the son of ex-NFLer Fred Jackson , returned a kickoff 99 yards against Michigan to get Iowa on the board in the first quarter.
Jackson was a star in his own right at Ankeny Centennial, setting a school record with 1,964 all-purpose yards as a senior and 27 touchdowns.
