After a wild first few weeks of the college football season, we may have our best slate yet in Week 4. Saturday features six matchups between teams ranked in the AP Top 25.
The day started with a marquee showdown between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee, and the Longhorns won rights to the 'UT' moniker with a tough defensive performance. Texas' Colin Simmons tied a school record with five sacks in a 20-17 win — though he did get in a bit of trouble after his first .
No. 17 Iowa provided the drama for the day in the afternoon, driving the length of the field in the final minute and scoring on a walk-off TD pass from Hank Brown to Reece Vander Zee as time expired to beat No. 18 Michigan 20-19 . Elsewhere, No. 4 Ole Miss got shelled by No. 21 Florida and No. 15 Utah held on for a 31-17 win at Iowa State .
In the evening, we have a trifecta of ranked-on-ranked matchups with No. 23 Texas A&M vs. No. 10 LSU, No. 20 Oregon vs. No. 12 USC and No. 19 Missouri vs. No. 24 Mississippi State. It's an action-packed slate that surely won't disappoint.
Follow all of the action with live updates, highlights and analysis below:
Right off the bat, new QB Dylan Raiola executes a play-fake and hits Evan Stewart for a 3-yard TD. Ducks take the lead.
Oregon 10, USC 7 | 2nd quarter
The Oregon QB was down on the field for a long time before he was taken off.
Backup QB Dylan Raiola will enter the game for the Ducks.
The Badgers completed the 17-point comeback and finish the upset. A stunner at Beaver Stadium.
It's been a defensive game thus far beyond the lone LSU touchdown drive, but A&M has some positive momentum heading into the second quarter after converting on a third-and-long out to near midfield.
Moore slid down after a run before USC's Desman Stephens laid a big hit to the QB's head. Moore is down on the field and a minor fight broke out after the play. That looked ugly. Stephens ejected with the targeting call.
Colton Joseph finds a completely wide open Jacob Harris, who rumbles 72 yards for the go-ahead score. Badgers are the verge of a big upset.
Wisconsin 24, Penn State 20 | 1:13 to play
Jayden Maiava drops a pinpoint pass to Kayden Dixon-Wyatt for a 31-yard scoring strike. Trojans take the lead.
After trailing 17-0 early, the Badgers have the ball with under 2 minutes, trailing 20-17. Can they pull the upset here?
Beyond that scoring drive from the Tigers, it's been a defensive affair early on in Baton Rouge.
A&M just got the ball back at its own 25.
Keelon Russell finds a wide open Ryan Coleman-Williams for a 32-yard TD and the Tide are up two scores early.

After LSU went 3-and-out on its first drive, it marched down the field for 8 plays and 82 yards, Dilin Jones finishes it with a 1-yard TD plunge.
The Ducks are on the board after a chip-shot field goal following a drive that got as far as the USC 7 before a holding penalty pushed them back.
The prime time SEC matchup has kicked off in Baton Rouge. LSU's offense gets the ball first.
The Trojans come up empty after a long drive as Caden Chittenden pushes his 33-yard attempt wide right.
The marquee Big Ten matchup of the day is underway in Los Angeles. USC starts with the ball.
The Tigers get their first SEC win under new head coach Alex Golesh
The Gators look for real as they improve to 4-0 with a dominant win over No. 4 Mississippi. Florida ran for 302 yards.
While the chaos was going on, the No. 2 Bulldogs cruised to a drama-free win over the reeling Sooners.
DJ Coleman picks off Ole Miss QB Trinidad Chambliss, and that puts an exclamation mark on this one.

articles.title_orig: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’
articles.title_zh: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’
articles.content_orig:
The humanistic heroes of the first film return, and so does writer-director Takashi Yamazaki's awesome sense of monster action paintings in motion.
Of all the criticisms leveled at Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (apart from the one I have: that the entire movie is a frigging mess), the most resonant, to me, was the complaint that Nolan had made a mistake by leaving the Greek gods out of the story. He certainly demonstrated that you could make a version of Homer minus the gods; he didn’t necessarily show that it could be done without losing a crucial dimension. Besides, if you can’t see gods at a movie of “The Odyssey,” where are you going to see them?
The answer is: at a Japanese monster movie — more thrilling, by leagues, than “The Odyssey” — where the monsters possess an ominous majesty that’s not of this world, even as they’re in the middle of laying waste to it.
In “ Godzilla Minus Zero ,” which premiered tonight at the New York Film Festival (it opens Nov. 6), there are two oversize mystic beasts: Godzilla, the original kaiju (the character is now 72 years old, proving that 72 is the new awesome), and King Ghidorah, the dragon hydra who made his first appearance in the 1964 kaiju classic “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster.” Each is a formidable creature, though in both cases it’s more than a matter of epic stomp or gargantuan wing power. When Godzilla tilts his head up to the sky, gathers his might, and then shoots out a blast of radioactivity that can level a city, it’s an exhibition of transcendent force . And Ghidorah’s heads — which look, up close, like costume figures out of a Golden Dragon Dance — emit orange lightning volts that extend for half a mile. These aren’t mere monsters. They’re serious movie gods.
“Godzilla Minus Zero” is set in 1949, and it opens with a startling sequence in which Ghidorah, with only one head (this will change), shows up in the city of Matsumoto and destroys it. We’re given a grand vista of demolition, and also close-ups of Ghidorah seen from the point-of-view of Professor Murakami (Min Tanaka), a Hiroshima survivor who’s been doing biological creature research. Godzilla will soon turn up as well, even though he was thought to have been destroyed at the end of “Godzilla Minus One.” (It’s hard to destroy a god.) To save Japan, Kenji Noda (Hidetake Yoshioka), the high-strung, pencil-necked, Einstein-haired director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, leads his team in devising a plan that’s got a sandbox-showdown ingenuity: They will lure both creatures to a single locale and goad them into fighting each other. Whichever one remains standing will be wounded and weakened, and the human forces can then finish that monster off.
When you go to see a big visual-effects movie, like something from Marvel, the closing credits that roll on for 12 minutes will feature multiple armies of visual-effects teams (each digital company with its own general). I have no doubt that a formidable army worked on “Godzilla Minus Zero.” But it’s also a movie that features the highly unusual credit “VFX, written, and directed by Takashi Yamazaki .” That’s a sign of how much the movie’s visual effects emanate directly from the imagination of the filmmaker. He’s writing, he’s directing, and he’s orchestrating spectacular gargantuan action paintings of beasts in motion. He’s an artist of larger-than-life pop horror.
We’ve seen countless monster duels in kaiju movies (old and new, good and bad, Japanese and American), but Yamazaki, who rebooted the genre and took it to a new peak in the revelatory 2023 retro kaiju classic “Godzilla Minus One,” works with a quality that none of the filmmakers of recent decades has summoned: a fairy-tale innocence, an immersion in the annihilating heavy-metal poetry of Godzilla — the way the destruction of a city can become a spectacle out of a dream (which is to say, a national nightmare). In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” when Godzilla and King Ghidorah go at it, it’s more than a WWE match of primeval rivals. It’s a clash of the titans that will reduce everyone in the audience to a wide-eyed, jaw-dropped child.
“Godzilla Minus One” was justly celebrated for its human story, which felt like something out of a Kurosawa movie of the ’50s. In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” Yamazaki follows through on that, continuing the tale of Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), the former World War II kamikaze pilot; Noriko (Minamo Hamabe), who is now his wife; and Akiko (Sae Nagatani), their adopted daughter, who has grown into a verbally precocious seven-year-old. The fate of this family is at the heart of the film’s emotional palette. To battle the creatures, Kōichi will go back into fighter-pilot mode, but the services of Noriko will be called on as well. She’s one of the survivors of Godzilla’s 1947 attack who now has bits of Godzilla DNA embedded in her body (which is why she wears an eyepatch).
For a long time, kaiju movies were a semi-joke — a fusion of the colossal and the cheesy, and the fact that you couldn’t separate the two was part of what gave the genre its unique shlock magic. But Yamazaki transcends all that. His staging draws on our collective nostalgic memory of kaiju grandeur, and it also dignifies the genre by building it on a drama that’s staged with passion and vigor. When did anyone ever talk about performances in a Godzilla movie? But in “Godzilla Minus Zero,” one responds to the high anxiety of Yoshioka’s Noda, and to the magnetic intelligence of Masami Nagasawa as Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist whose intuition about storms has a hint of the prophetic. Min Tanaka, who plays the professor, is an actor who was born on March 10, 1945, the day of the firebombing of Tokyo (the deadliest air raid in human history), and his courtly but simmering presence powerfully channels the film’s awareness of history. Yamazaki stages a couple of audacious sequences that feel, in their way, like his answer to “Oppenheimer.” One is a fantasy of Godzilla approaching Manhattan the way he once approached Tokyo, a chilling vision for any American to behold.
At first, when the Japanese officials think that they’re contending only with Ghidorah, the film’s battles have a tactical stateliness. Ghidorah heads off to the mountains and hibernates, curling up like a giant snake, which makes them think they can bomb him into oblivion, using planes and weapons borrowed from the U.S. But all that accomplishes is to wake the sleeping giant. The sequence in which a half dozen planes battle Ghidorah in the air is grand, eye-popping filmmaking. And that’s just the appetizer, as Godzilla’s return heralds a battle of staggering vastness.
In the final section, a plot strand or two gets a bit tangled. The professor has a hidden agenda, and how he ever meant to carry it out remains too abstract to be entirely clear. Yet as key characters are put under fire, we realize how much we’ve come to care about these creature battlers. They’re rooted in a time and place that feels all too real, and this allows the monsters to parade their primitive might in a way that means something. It was a stroke of inspiration on Yamazaki’s part to reset the kaiju genre in the late ’40s, during the Atomic Age where it is spiritually rooted (the original “Gojira” was released in 1954). The creators of the new James Bond series would do well to follow suit. (That’s how Bond could be vital again.) “Godzilla Minus Zero” is destined to connect with a huge international audience, and it’s already clear that this won’t be the last of Yamazaki’s kaiju epics. That’s because the movie proves that when you do it right, what seemed old can become timeless.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
Using a controversial move known as a “pocket rescission,” Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children.

Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is “consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.”
In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.”
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.
A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.
The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).
The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.
Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.
It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.
The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.”
“If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues.
Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA.
“It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.”
The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.
In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.
The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says.
He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.
Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’”
The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.
The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.
The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.”
The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.
“I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.”
The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.
“If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks.
The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

articles.title_zh: US got pandas from China. Trump needs a lot more than that | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_orig: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.title_zh: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: Florida surges into CFP conversation after trouncing Ole Miss as Jon Sumrall eyes SEC coaching history
articles.title_zh: Florida surges into CFP conversation after trouncing Ole Miss as Jon Sumrall eyes SEC coaching history
articles.content_orig:
We'll be seeing ample Gator chomps the rest of the way this season.
Coming out of Saturday's 52-28 statement win over previously unbeaten and No. 4 Ole Miss , the No. 21 Gators look the part in the early season College Football Playoff conversation and have a surging Heisman candidate leading their backfield in Jadan Baugh .
Jon Sumrall is trying to become the fifth first-year coach all-time to reach the CFP in his first campaign. He'd join four others across the Power Four to accomplish that feat, but would make history as the first from the SEC.
The win for the Gators snapped a four-game losing skid against ranked competition and was Florida's first victory over a top-five opponent since 2020 ( Georgia ).
The Gators had lost their previous 12 matchups against the nation's elite, and Sumrall joked that, coming into Saturday's showdown, his team has no business being favored against the Rebels .
The telling sign of a well-coached team with no signs of wilting is its ability to respond, and the Gators reflected that in the third quarter, absorbing body blows before punching back.
Florida broke open a 24-21 game in the second half with consecutive touchdown drives predicated by the power running of Baugh and Duke Clark along with quarterback Aaron Philo's precision on third down.
Ole Miss entered Week 4 with the SEC's worst rush defense, giving up 159 yards per game, and nothing changed inside Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Baugh and Clark combined for 268 yards on the ground, both eclipsing the 100-yard barrier — the first time that's happened in the same game for Florida since 2022.
That's part of the new identity Sumrall mentioned earlier this week.
"I think our mindset has changed," Sumrall said. "I think we're playing with a different level of resiliency and toughness than what I felt like was going on here when I got here. And I think our guys expect to win. So that's one component I think that I'm pleased with. How we play the game, some detail, some consistency.
"There's a lot of areas where you still have to improve upon a lot to become the type of team we want to be long term. And so we're a long way from a finished product here. We haven't even begun to scratch the surface for what my vision is for how we play this game week in, week out."
That's two SEC tests and two wins for a first-year coach who has Florida looking like a factor — not only in the SEC race — in the national championship discussion. Sumrall inherited a talented roster, but he deserves credit for getting this much out of it this quickly.
For the first time since 2021, Florida will be a top-15 team in Sunday's new AP poll entering October with all of the program's lofty goals still out front. It's a weekly grind in the SEC, and anything can happen over the Gators' final eight games, but this looks like a team capable of reaching the CFP and being a tough out, given this roster embodies its coach's mindset.
Sumrall said his players looked "a little bit over-amped" after the first quarter ended with a failed fourth-and-2 conversion try at the Rebels' 19-yard line. Florida had a comfortable 10-point lead, and Philo had a man open in the flat for a potential touchdown but failed to execute.
In the past, the Gators' offense might have folded after that or struggled to regain confidence with Trinidad Chambliss and an elite passing game on the other sideline. However, all of the opposition's counter jabs were answered with force as Florida barged its way into the national spotlight.
With Buster Faulkner calling the plays and a renewed focus on physicality off the snap, the Gators are scoring points in bunches with an onslaught of explosive plays. Florida's 214 points are the most through the first four games of a season since 1996 — when the Gators won the national title under Steve Spurrier.
Elite territory for Sumrall and Co.

articles.title_orig: Trump turns on Salazar after Florida Republican challenges his immigration crackdown
articles.title_zh: Trump turns on Salazar after Florida Republican challenges his immigration crackdown
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Florida, has made waves by publicly breaking with President Donald Trump over immigration.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in a new campaign ad . "The same Hispanics that helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
In 2024, voters broadly trusted Republicans to handle illegal immigration. Through incompetence and cruelty, the Trump administration has lost that goodwill. The last election showed Republicans have a path forward on immigration. But to take it, they need to ditch the cruel memes and aggressive tactics that have plagued Trump's second term.
Salazar is right: Hispanics were a major part of Trump's 2024 victory. According to Pew Research Center, the president nearly tied former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, a group former President Joe Biden won by 25 percentage points in 2020.
Since then, Trump's gains among Hispanics have evaporated. In February 2025, according to Pew , 93% of Hispanics who voted for Trump approved of the job he was doing. By April of this year, just 66% did. Over the same stretch, his approval among all Hispanic adults fell from 36% to 22%, while among non-Hispanic adults, it slipped from 49% to 37%.
The drop in support can be attributed largely to the administration's mishandling of immigration.
The loudest headlines came out of Operation Metro Surge, the enforcement campaign that flooded Minneapolis with more than 3,000 federal agents last winter. The surge was driven more by political optics than by any strategic need, and it ended with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Worse yet, administration officials then smeared Pretti . White House advisor Stephen Miller called him a "domestic terrorist," and the Department of Homeland Security claimed he "wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement." Bystander video showed he never drew his holstered pistol, which he was licensed to carry. Americans noticed: 61% of voters told Quinnipiac University pollsters that the administration had not given an honest account of the shooting.
Previously: We need to change the way we talk about the ICE shooting | Opinion
By mid-February, Americans opposed ICE's tactics 62% to 31%, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. The backlash presumably helped cost Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem her job.
Since Noem's firing, ICE has largely faded from the headlines, as DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin has worked to keep the agency out of the spotlight. That changed Sept. 20, when an ICE officer in Austin shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan man with a deportation order who had fled a vehicle stop. The facts are still unclear, and there is no ICE body-camera footage of the shooting. After Minneapolis, Americans have little reason to give the administration the benefit of the doubt.
Opinion alerts: Get columns from your favorite columnists + expert analysis on top issues, delivered straight to your device through the USA TODAY app. Don't have the app? Download it for free from your app store .
Beyond the heated environment it needlessly created in Minnesota, the administration has driven support away with its messaging.
Throughout Trump's second term, official government social media accounts have churned out memes , many of them about immigration. The White House posted a Studio Ghibli-style cartoon of a convicted drug trafficker weeping as she was arrested and has promised that "the memes will continue." Other posts have included mock travel ads for deportation flights, and the administration has co-opted endless TikTok memes and audio trends to celebrate deportations.
All of it undercuts the administration's posture on such a serious matter. Nobody has ever been won over to a policy by a cartoon of a crying deportee, criminal or not. All it does is deepen the divide.
Austin ICE shooting proves we've lost ability to wait for facts | Opinion
Frustration with Democrats' failures at the border handed Republicans an opening in 2024. Voters trusted Trump over Harris on immigration 51% to 38%. Republicans have since squandered that advantage, but the path to a sensible immigration policy isn't closed.

The man who was injured in the shooting was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by Austin immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who said she was hired to represent him.
The incident was followed by a swift reaction from elected officials, as the public protested the latest shooting involving federal officers in the United States this year.

Americans still draw a line between securing the border and Trump's broader crackdown. In a New York Times/Siena College poll in January, roughly half of voters approved of his handling of the border, while they were split on deportations and a clear majority said ICE had "gone too far." That gap shows sensible border policy still has broad support, despite the administration's spectacle of mismanagement and cruelty.
Trump's inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024 were thought to signal a new Republican coalition, and they showed that these voters could back a more conservative immigration policy. Those gains have all but vanished. What looked like a lasting Republican asset has become a serious liability heading into the midterms.
To win back their advantage on immigration, Republicans need to ditch the cruelty. The memes, ICE's aggressive tactics and the general callousness have soured Americans on policies that should command popular support for years to come.
Lawmakers like Salazar may be breaking with Trump for electoral reasons. But if they win in November, they will be the ones building the Republican Party's next approach to immigration. That approach should press Democrats on their weaknesses on the issue, without the cruelty that has defined Trump's second term.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents probed US government sites in unexpected ways
articles.title_zh: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents probed US government sites in unexpected ways
articles.content_orig:
Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face , a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

Hurricane Nolo expected to strengthen to a Category 3, south of Hawaii
Hurricane Nolo continues to move west as it lashes the Big Island of Hawaii with torrential rain, winds and dangerous surf.
Nolo is expected to strengthen to a major hurricane by Sunday as it moves south of the island chain.
The storm has begun to move westward away from the Big Island at about 8mph. All tropical storm and hurricane watches and warnings have been discontinued. They have been replaced with high wind warnings for portions of the Big Island and Maui County, where gusts up to 75 mph are possible.
Pockets of heavy rain are expected to expand across the rest of the Big Island and Maui. Strong winds are  currently gusting across the Big Island and in some wind-prone areas of Maui County, Oahu and Kauai.
Rainfall totals over 12 inches have been reported on the Big Island.
Nolo continues to move west after being stationary for hours on Saturday. The storm should move into warmer water during the next 24 hours, which will help it intensify into a major hurricane on Sunday or Monday.

( MORE: What a forecast cone really means )
For now, the forecast keeps the core of Nolo — and thus the worst of its wind impacts — south of the islands.
Parts of the islands will continue to see the triple threat of rain, winds and waves, regardless of how close Nolo's center tracks to the Big Island.
As the storm passes south of the islands, heavy rain will continue to impact parts of the Big Island, Maui, Lanai, Molokai and Kahoolawe. Flood watches remain in effect for those areas.
Here are the peak rainfall forecasts from NOAA's Weather Prediction Center. These peak totals are most possible over mountain slopes:
This could lead to life-threatening, potentially catastrophic flash flooding and mudslides on the Big Island and life-threatening flooding and mudslides on Maui, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Hawaii’s higher terrain can squeeze more moisture as storm's outer bands pass, enhancing the rainfall along the slopes andincreasing the risk for mudslides and faster runoff.  That water flows downhill where lower elevated communities could face both flash flooding and debris flows.
Be aware that the flooding and debris can travel well beyond where the heaviest rain falls.
The Big Island and parts of Maui County were hit hard by flooding, mudslides and strong winds from Hurricane Lala in mid-August, and some places just recently got power restored.
The best chance of winds capable of at least some tree damage and power outages is expected across parts of the Big Island and Maui County
In addition, wind gusts will likely be stronger both at the tops of and downwind of mountain slopes in the entire island chain.
Coastal flooding, high surf
Larger swells are producing dangerous surf and rip currents.
Nolo will continue to bring a threat of coastal flooding to parts of the Big Island through the weekend.
Only one other major (Category 3 or stronger) hurricane has tracked within 150 miles of the Big Island, according to NOAA's hurricane database.
That was August 1959's Hurricane Dot, which went on to slam into Kauai after brushing south of the Big Island.
So Nolo is the strongest Big Island impact from a hurricane in 67 years.
This system will become the fourth to at least graze Hawaii, bringing flooding and winds to most of the state.
We first had Hurricane Lala in mid-August, whose eyewall grazed the southern end of the Big Island. Torrential rain hit, and gusty winds caused power outages to skyrocket.
Next up was Tropical Storm Moke, which tracked farther south than Lala but still hit parts of the Big Island with rain and winds from its outer bands. Moke’s impacts were less significant, but flooding still occurred because the ground was still saturated from Lala.
Then there was Hurricane Lowell, a powerful hurricane that reached Category 5 strength at its peak. The storm weakened before making its closest pass, but it slammed the western islands with wind, rain and waves.

articles.title_orig: No. 1 Texas, Arch Manning outlast No. 14 Tennessee: How Horns survived Vols’ late surge
articles.title_zh: No. 1 Texas, Arch Manning outlast No. 14 Tennessee: How Horns survived Vols’ late surge
articles.content_orig:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — Colin Simmons tied the program record with five sacks as top-ranked Texas held off No. 14 Tennessee 20-17 Saturday with President Donald Trump on hand in the Longhorns’ first visit to Neyland Stadium.
Raleek Brown ran for 67 yards and a pair of touchdowns, and his 4-yarder with 5:41 left gave the Longhorns the winning margin in the Southeastern Conference opener for both teams. Giannis Spetic had a pair of field goals.
It was a defensive day with Texas (4-0) dominating with 10 sacks, led by Simmons. The linebacker’s day for the record books also will be remembered for his vulgar celebration after one sack. He was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct with the referee saying Simmons was “simulating” using the restroom.
Tennessee quarterback Brandon Faizon made it interesting late, capping an 80-yard drive with a 30-yard TD pass to Mike Matthews with 1:22 left. Linebacker Arion Carter recovered the onside kick, and Jelani McDonald batted away Brandon’s pass to Travis Smith Jr. on the final play in the end zone.
NO. 2 GEORGIA 41, OKLAHOMA 13
ATHENS, Ga. — Chris Cole scored on a 85-yard fumble return as Georgia took advantage of three first-half turnovers by John Mateer and overwhelmed struggling Oklahoma.
Mateer lost two fumbles, each recovered by Cole, and threw an interception in the first half as Oklahoma (2-2, 0-1 Southeastern Conference) fell behind 28-0. K.J. Bolden picked off a pass from Mateer in the second quarter.
While Mateer struggled with turnovers, Gunner Stockton was almost perfect in the first half for Georgia (4-0, 2-0). Stockton completed his first nine passes, including a 35-yard touchdown throw to Talyn Taylor.
The Sooners finished with four turnovers, including a fumble by tight end Rocky Beers in the third quarter.
Mateer’s second lost fumble, forced by Raylen Wilson, was returned 23 yards by Cole late in the first half to set up Chauncey Bowens’ second touchdown run.
Georgia rolled despite holding out its top running back, Nate Frazier, due to injured ribs. Bowens had touchdown runs of 2 and 6 yards as the fill-in starter. Dwight Phillips added a 54-yard touchdown run early in the fourth quarter.
NO. 3 NOTRE DAME 49, PURDUE 10
WEST LAFAYETTE, Ind. — CJ Carr threw three touchdown passes and ran for another score, linebacker Drayk Bowen scored his first career TD on a 15-yard fumble return and Notre Dame beat Purdue.
Carr was 14 of 22 for 237 yards and threw his first interception of the season. It’s the second straight week Carr has had a TD pass and a TD run in the same game. Aneyas Williams carried 14 times for 80 yards with one TD as the Fighting Irish (4-0) produced a season-high 177 yards rushing.
Notre Dame has won 14 straight and will start October with a perfect record for the first time since 2021.
It was another miserable day for the struggling Boilermakers (1-3). Ryan Browne was 18 of 28 for 111 yards and lost the fumble that Bowen returned for the touchdown. Purdue had only 12 yards rushing in the first half and finished the game with only 218 total yards as it lost its third straight.
NO. 21 FLORIDA 52, NO. 4 MISSISSIPPI 28
GAINESVILLE, Fla. — Jadan Baugh ran for 142 yards and three touchdowns, Duke Clark added 126 yards and a score on the ground, and Florida manhandled Mississippi to reach 4-0 for the first time since 2019.
The Gators (4-0, 2-0 Southeastern Conference), installed as 3 1/2-point favorites, proved Las Vegas oddsmakers right by leading from start to finish. They scored touchdowns on five consecutive drives in the second half.
The Rebels (3-1, 1-1) insisted that last week’s victory against LSU, the one that spoiled former Ole Miss coach Lane Kiffin’s return, was not their “Super Bowl.” But they failed to build off that emotional win.
Florida had a lot to do with it.
The Gators jumped on the Rebels early, leading 10-0 before Heisman Trophy front-runner Trinidad Chambliss even threw a pass, and set the pace the rest of the afternoon. Florida was unstoppable running the ball.
NO. 7 OHIO ST. 42, ILLINOIS 19
COLUMBUS, Ohio — Jeremiah Smith tied an Ohio State record with four touchdown catches and also had career highs with 12 receptions for 217 yards as the Buckeyes beat Illinois.
According to Sportradar, it is the 23rd time since 2000 a FBS player has had double-digit catches for at least 200 yards and four scores in a game. The last to do it was Western Michigan’s Sky Moore against Northern Illinois in 2021.
It is the fifth time an Ohio State receiver has had four touchdowns. The last time it happened before Saturday was Noah Brown at Oklahoma in 2016.
It also tied for the sixth-most receiving yards in an OSU game and tied for sixth-most receptions.
Smith tied the mark with 10:07 remaining in the fourth quarter when he was wide open on a 26-yard touchdown to extend the Buckeyes’ lead to 35-13.
Smith also became the third receiver since 2015 from a Power Four conference to have at least three games with at least 150 receiving yards and two touchdowns in one half. DeVonta Smith had four at Alabama and Ja’Marr Chase did it three times at LSU.
NO. 11 TEXAS TECH 49, SAM HOUSTON 14
LUBBOCK, Texas — Texas Tech linebacker Austin Romaine became the first FBS player in 13 years to return two interceptions for touchdowns on consecutive throws, Cameron Dickey ran for two scores and the Red Raiders beat Sam Houston.
Both pick-6s by Romaine came in the opening minute of the second quarter, and were against different quarterbacks.
The Red Raiders (4-0) extended their home winning streak to 11 games, their longest since 12 in a row from 2007-09.
A nearly five TD favorite, Texas Tech led only 21-14 at halftime before Dickey’s second scoring run, a 13-yarder, and Will Hammond’s 21-yard TD to Coy Eakin in the first five minutes after the break.
Hammond finished 17-of-29 passing for 224 yards, but threw three interceptions in the final 5 1/2 minutes of the first half — though Sam Houston (1-3) got only seven points off those. Hammond added a 23-yard TD run in the fourth quarter.
NO. 15 UTAH 31, IOWA ST. 17
AMES, Iowa — Wayshawn Parker broke a 54-yard run on the game’s opening play from scrimmage for the first of his three touchdowns and Utah held off Iowa State in the second half to beat the Cyclones.
Parker rushed for a career-high 174 yards and two TDs on 18 carries and caught five passes for 65 yards and a score for the Utes (4-0, 1-0 Big 12).
Jaylen Raynor got the Cyclones (2-2, 0-1) within 24-17 early in the fourth quarter, scoring on an 8-yard run and throwing a 22-yard touchdown pass to Dominic Overby after Overby had stretched the ball over the line to convert a fourth-and-12 on the previous play.
The Utes punted on their first three series of the second half and then put away the Cyclones with a 61-yard drive ending with Devon Dampier’s 13-yard TD pass to Parker and Jackson Bennett’s interception on the first play of Iowa State’s ensuing possession.
Parker led a Utah rushing attack that finished with 206 yards, and Dampier was 18 of 27 for 206 yards and two TDs.
WAKE FOREST 30, NO. 16 LOUISVILLE 27
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Connor Calvert kicked three field goals, including a 32-yarder with 6:20 remaining, to lift Wake Forest to a 30-27 upset win over Louisville.
Gio Lopez threw for 225 yards and a touchdown on 12 of 19 passing for the Demon Deacons (3-1, 1-1 Atlantic Coast Conference), who scored their first conference win of the season. Carlos Hernandez caught nine of those for 194 yards, just three yards off the career best he set last season against Delaware.
Ty Clark III carried the ball 21 times for 91 yards and two touchdowns.

The duo connected on a 77-yard touchdown pass to put the Demon Deacons up 17-14 with 5:49 left in the first half. articles.title_orig: Iowa vs Michigan recap: Iowa wins with last-second TD, 20-19
articles.title_zh: Iowa vs Michigan recap: Iowa wins with last-second TD, 20-19
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
articles.title_zh: Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
articles.content_orig:
China touts multilateralism and growing soft power even as Beijing gives greater weight to its relationship with Washington
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.
“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has addressed the annual General Assembly gathering once in person, in 2015 for the 70th anniversary. He appeared by video in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic but missed the 80th anniversary last year when Premier Li Qiang spoke. In other years, China has generally been represented by other senior officials, including Han and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

articles.title_orig: 87-year-old woman's eviction from Madrid apartment sparks protest against Spain's housing crisis
articles.title_zh: 87-year-old woman's eviction from Madrid apartment sparks protest against Spain's housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets in Madrid on Saturday to protest against Spain’s housing crisis and ask for protective measures for tenants, anti-fraud rules, and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.
The protest came in reaction to the dramatic eviction on Wednesday of an 87-year-old woman from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for decades.
“We’re here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes,” said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. “And we can’t keep maintaining this. Housing is a right and we don’t have it.”
Taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood, María del Carmen Abascal was greeted by protesters and supporters as she was loaded into an ambulance.
Spanish media reported that Abascal’s father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a rent cap.
The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organized Saturday’s protest .
Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.
Courts blocked three previous attempts to evict her. Extensive media coverage turned Abascal into a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis.
“This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we’ve been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now,” said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher. “It’s unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can’t afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted.”
At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza with apparent plans to stay put. Some even pitched tents to stay at least the night — or until police forcibly removed them.
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market , despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace. Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.
The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.
Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of its available supply. The European Union average is 8%.
Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership, removing them from the public housing stock.
“I haven’t managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what’s theirs,” Abascal said in a video shared on Friday by the tenants’ union. The video was recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction.

articles.title_orig: NFL says Maracanã Stadium field passed required tests before Cowboys-Ravens kickoff
articles.title_zh: NFL says Maracanã Stadium field passed required tests before Cowboys-Ravens kickoff
articles.content_orig:
The playing surface at Brazil's Maracanã Stadium passed all testing Friday following concerns voiced by the NFL Players Association.
NFL field director Nick Pappas met with reporters on Saturday, one day before the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys are set to play . Pappas said that all mandatory requirements have been met regarding the surface, and testing was done in conjunction with the NFLPA and an independent specialist.
"We have an independent inspector that comes in, walks with myself, walks with a member of the NFLPA," Pappas said. "They were here yesterday. Performed that test. Things check out. We've made additional improvements to the field that we think were helpful."
However, close-up footage taken by Dallas' 105.3 The Fan showed several very thin patches on the field with sparse tufts of grass sprouting up from green-colored dirt.
Pappas added that the league has visited the stadium once a month since January for regular checkups. The region has seen a lot of rainfall of late, plus games played by soccer clubs Flamengo and Fluminense, including one last Sunday.
"I mean rest was No. 1, right?" Pappas said about the work that's been done since last weekend. "Giving the opportunity to get some rest, made a phone call to shut the rain off. So we've got some sunshine now. I wish I could take credit for that. Stitching was a big piece of it, but then also bringing in the field goal posts, getting the lines and getting things measured out and laid out. There's got to be a football field out here too."
On Friday, NFLPA executive director JC Tretter posted a lengthy statement on social media , including what has needed to be addressed with the grass playing surface in Rio de Janeiro leading up to kickoff on Sunday.
"The concern heading into this week was that the field would be loose, patchy, and lead to excessive slipping," Tretter wrote. "Those conditions are generally more of a playability and performance issue than a significant injury concern."
Tretter added that safety is the primary issue for players. But a surface that allows them to perform at their highest level, resulting in a well-played game, is also a major consideration.
Both the league and experts hired by the NFLPA have checked the field during the past week and found that the grass surface wasn't stable enough to be suitable for a game. The latest assessment means they will definitely play football there on Sunday.
The Cowboys arrived at the stadium on Saturday for a walkthrough to test out the surface. Some players, like CeeDee Lamb , went barefoot . Others, like kicker Brandon Aubrey , wore cleats to get a better idea of how the footing will hold up.
Kickoff is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET on Sunday with the Cowboys serving as the home team.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Plans to Gut Clean Car Rules
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Plans to Gut Clean Car Rules
articles.content_orig:
Tesla Supercharger StationTesla Model Y electric vehicle connected to a Tesla Supercharger in a shopping center parking lot, Walnut Creek, California, September 14, 2026. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump has signed off on new fuel economy standards that he claims will end a Biden-era push for carmakers to build more electric vehicles.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Transportation is expected to approve new, dramatically reduced emissions standards that will last through 2031. In a post announcing his support for the move, Trump said "these new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America."
"That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car – Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore," Trump wrote in his post. "Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!"
Trump blasted the current fuel economy standards, arguing that they cost manufacturers billions of dollars, wasted billions on chargers, and forced people to buy vehicles that they did not want.
The new standards are expected to cut the cost of building new vehicles, but will drive up fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, the U.S. Department of Transportation predicts.
RELATED: Trump rescinds nearly $1B in funds approved by Congress: Why senators say it's illegal
According to Reuters , the new proposal would require an automaker’s fleetwide fuel economy average to be 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031, a sharp decrease from the 50.4 miles per gallon under the current regulations.
Reducing the restrictions is predicted to shave $930 off the cost of an average new vehicle, Reuters reported. Conversely, the new standards are expected to result in 100 billion more gallons of fuel to be consumed, an extra $185 billion spent on fuel, and an increase in carbon dioxide emissions by 5%, according to DOT numbers.
Reuters quoted former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who led the agency under President Joe Biden, as saying "lowering standards will accelerate what (Trump) has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump."
The Source: Information for this article was taken from FOX Business, Reuters, President Donald Trump’s Truth Social post, and the U.S. Department of Transportation. This story was reported from Orlando.

articles.title_zh: New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson kicks off the new season of ‘SNL’ tonight
articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, is slated to kick off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live” on Saturday, the show said.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday is Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

SEAL BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- If you are thinking about heading to the beach, you might want to reconsider -- along with big waves, Hurricane Polo could bring dangerous rip currents, flooding and more erosion to Southern California.
High sand berms line up the shoreline, protecting homes in Seal Beach as residents there prepare for another storm heading their way.
Although SoCal shores will not get hit directly by Hurricane Polo, heading towards Mexico, its impact will still be felt in our region, especially at south-facing beaches. Those areas could see waves up to 7 feet tall or higher in the coming days.
Flooding, high surf and dangerous rip currents are expected, along with seeing more beach erosion.
Residents preparing for the upcoming storm are hoping the built-up sand berms and other preparations make a difference this time around.
"I think they're gonna hold, because we weren't  prepared, I don't think Seal Beach was prepared for the last one," said area resident Susana Villalon.
"If you go down to Aliso Creek Beach, you can see how much the sand disappeared," said Laguna Beach resident Trish Sweeney. "And we lost quit a bit of sand over the years...shown how much damage it is."
The peninsula in Long Beach, another community hit hard by the effects of Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend, has been closed for public safety and residents were urged to stay off sand berms and avoid areas where heavy equipment is operating.
City officials were urging residents to prepare for high tides, large swells and possible coastal flooding from swells generated by Hurricane Polo, with the greatest flooding risk expected Monday and Tuesday.
The Long Beach City Council ratified a proclamation of a local emergency so they can activate the resources they need to head ahead of this storm.
Local fire departments are also on high alert. Ready-to-fill sandbags are available at all Los Angeles Fire Department neighborhood fire stations -- up to 25 bags per household.
A beach hazard statement is going to be in effect through Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: Japanese Naval Strengthening Steals Limelight at U.S.-China Talks
articles.content_orig:
Published
					Sep 26, 2026 6:37 PM        		by The Maritime Executive
Chinese criticism of Japan’s growing defense budget appears to have been one of the most consequential developments coming out of the days President Xi Jinping spent in Washington for his state visit, which otherwise seems to have done little to move forward Sino-US relations. In advance of the meeting, Chinese Ambassador to Washington Xie Feng had warned that President Xi should not be challenged over Taiwan, democracy and human rights, nor restrictions to China’s growing development influence in the world, so the agenda between the two presidents was limited.
Japan’s Sanae Takaichi was in New York at the same time to make her first appearance as Prime Minister at the UN General Assembly, and held bilateral meetings with President Trump in New York. Chinese state media chose the moment of the Sino-US summit to launch a stinging attack on Prime Minister Takaichi’s radical plans to increase Japanese defense spending, and in particular to strengthen naval and air defense forces defending Japan’s isolated southern islands, specifically the Nansei Chain islands of Miyako, Ishigaki and Yonaguni.
Japan’s possession of these islands, and others to the east and north-east of Taiwan, would prove an obstacle to any Chinese plan to invade Taiwan. If long-range anti-aircraft and anti-shipping missiles are stationed on these islands, they would be able to disrupt the deployment of the PLA Navy to encircle Taiwan and cut it off from external reinforcement.
Prime Minister Takaichi has already made it clear that a Chinese invasion of Taiwan would be a causus belli for Japan, and a strategic threat to Japan’s national security. Her approach has been endorsed in this year’s general election in Japan, which gave her an unprecedented supermajority in the Japanese Diet, sufficient to change the constitution and to support a doubling of the percentage of GDP devoted to defense.
Besides a significant expansion of the Japan Maritime Self Defense Force, in particular enhancements to its Mogami Class frigates and submarine fleet, the Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Minister Koizumi has already announced that infrastructure to support a permanent presence of Chu-SAM (Type-03) medium-range air defense missiles on the Japanese island of Yonaguni will be in place by 2030. Field-deployed Chu-SAM systems are probably there already, with sufficient range to cover the eastern approaches to Taiwan.

These systems will thicken up air defense cover for the Okinawa-based 12th Marine Littoral Regiment, which is tasked alongside the JGSDF with defending Japan’s outlying islands, and which has recently been re-equipped with the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction Systems (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated Systems (MADIS). Mobile Japanese Type 88 coastal defense anti-ship missile systems can also be expected to be deployed to the islands, and all these systems have ranges which cover Taiwan’s eastern flank and coastal areas.
The Chinese diplomatic assault on Japan was headlined in the Chinese Military Bugle newspaper, which told its readers that China had rights over Japan, because Japan is still defined by the United Nations - as it has been since 1945 - as an ‘enemy country’, entitling China to take unilateral action if it feels threatened. The same paper criticized Japan for its Free and Open Indo-Pacific project, which looks very similar to the Chinese Belt and Road outreach program combining security and economic development objectives. The Chinese defense spokesperson upbraided Japan for supporting Filipino protests over aggressive Chinese coastguard actions off the Spratly Islands, over which the Japanese Embassy in the Philippines had said it was "gravely concerned". The Xi-Trump talks attracted one story in the Chinese Military Bugle, whilst China’s criticism of Japan was covered in four stories.

articles.title_orig: Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend
articles.title_zh: Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend
articles.content_orig:
John Garrisi, left, and Gaige Graf move an outdoor table away from the shorefront during the early stages of a nor'easter storm on Friday. Robert F. Bukaty/AP hide caption
Talia Manno opened her door on Saturday morning to waves lapping halfway up the front steps to her Atlantic City, N.J., home.
"It got up to my fifth step," Manno said. "I was really freaking out."
Manno, a lifelong resident, said the last time water came that high was during Hurricane Sandy .
"Even if you live here and you see high tide and flooding, that was really scary and it happened so fast," she said.
Manno is among tens of millions of people from the mid-Atlantic through the coast of Maine who are in the path of a powerful and rare September nor'easter that is bringing coastal flooding, heavy rain and high winds this weekend.
Nearly 80,000 people were without power across New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and Massachusetts, as of Saturday evening, according to the PowerOutage.com map. The storm is expected to continue hitting the Jersey Shore, New York City, and Eastern Massachusetts into Sunday, according to NWS.
Videos posted on social media Saturday showed streets inundated with water in New Jersey, and massive waves hitting the coast . In New York City, people were seen kayaking in the streets . New Jersey and New York declared states of emergency in counties across the two states, including in New York City.
Francis Tarasiewicz, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Massachusetts, said wind gusts along the coast could reach up to 60 miles per hour this weekend. This nor'easter comes earlier than the typical October through May storm season, he said, and will last longer than normal.
Spectators watch wave break during a nor'easter storm on Saturday in Hampton, N.H. Robert F. Bukat/AP hide caption
"Many nor'easters affect the area over the course of about a day," he said. "It's a quick punch of strong winds, in many cases, heavy snow or rain." But, Tarasiewicz said, "with this one, we're looking at about a 48-hour period of winds greater than 35 to 40 miles per hour across the area."
The nor'easter is also making travel difficult. More than 1,000 flights were canceled Saturday with thousands more delayed, according to data from FlightAware . Ferry services on Cape Cod and in Rhode Island were disrupted, and Amtrak canceled several trains due to the weather and downed wires.
Off the coast of New York, the strong winds made for a rough cruise ride for Jessica Lisboa. She brought green apples, ginger ale and an acupressure anti-nausea bracelet to prepare for the Bermuda-bound cruise.
"Let me not sugarcoat it. Was it wild? Yeah, sure. It was a little wild," Lisboa said. "It felt honestly like a roller coaster." Still, she considered it a worthwhile adventure.
The nor'easter also took out a number of events planned for the weekend. Oceans Calling, one of Maryland's biggest music festivals, was canceled on Friday. An AC/DC concert in New Jersey was rescheduled. The Boston Red Sox announced they would move their game against the Chicago Cubs.
Some East Coasters found a way to adapt.
When Olga Ostrovetsky picked a date in September for her small outdoor wedding, she envisioned a beautiful, fall day.
But as she got ready to tie the knot in Wallkill, N.Y., she said, "It's very, very windy."
At first bummed, she's now finding the positives in the disruption.
"It's kind of fitting, to be honest, because my fiancé and I met and it was a torrential downpour," she said. "We met on a day like this, and we're also getting married on a day like this," she said.
As for Manno, the Atlantic City resident, is planning to spend Saturday night with family away from the coast. After this nor'easter, she said she doesn't know how much longer she'll live in the area.
"As the years pass, it seems like it's just getting more and more flooding," she said. "It's crazy."

articles.title_zh: Social media platforms refuse to run paid ads for 'Musk' documentary
articles.content_orig:
Musk , Alex Gibney's four-hour documentary about Elon Musk , hits theaters in two weeks and received rave reviews out of its premiere at the Venice International Film Festival. Yet distributor Bleecker Street can't buy ads on major social media platforms in order to promote it.
According to The Hollywood Reporter , YouTube , TikTok , and Meta , which owns Instagram and Facebook , have all refused to run the trailer for Musk . The same goes for X, which is owned by Musk and which reportedly won't accept advertising for Bleecker Street's other upcoming releases.
YouTube, TikTok, and Meta told Bleecker Street representatives that they rejected the trailer because of "political content." TikTok and Meta do not allow paid political and campaign ads, with Meta's rules stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. YouTube does, with ads requiring "paid for" disclosures. The Musk trailer contains references to the 2024 election, but it is not itself a political campaign.
Bleecker Street has appealed YouTube, TikTok, and Meta's decision. While YouTube and TikTok are still mulling over the request, Meta has rejected it outright.
This isn't the first bump in the road for Musk . Universal Pictures, which is distributing the film internationally, reportedly got cold feet on releasing Musk . Evan Langweiler, Universal's Executive Vice President of Global Communications and Media Relations, has since told The Hollywood Reporter that , "the studio remains committed to releasing [ Musk ] in theaters internationally."
The incident recalls Amazon MGM Studios' dropping of Luca Guadagnino's OpenAI and Sam Altman film Artificial , another fall release that looks to take a prominent tech figure to task. Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning , also out this fall, will follow a similar path with Mark Zuckerberg.
